# Deuteronomy Chapter 34 — SOPHIA Consensus Translation

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **Sources:** EMET (literal), LOGOS (formal), PNEUMA (dynamic) | **Base text:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 234–235 | **LXX:** Codex Vaticanus (Vat.gr.1209), pp. 169–170
**Disagreement Log:** `disagreements/DEU_034.md`

---

**1** Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho. And the LORD showed him all the land — Gilead as far as Dan, **2** and all of Naphtali, and the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, and all the land of Judah as far as the Western Sea, **3** and the Negev, and the plain — the Valley of Jericho, the city of palm trees — as far as Zoar.

**4** And the LORD said to him, "This is the land of which I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, 'I will give it to your offspring.' I have let you see it with your eyes, but you shall not cross over there."

**5** So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word [literally: mouth — al pi YHWH] of the LORD. **6** And he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab opposite Beth-peor; but no one knows the place of his burial to this day. **7** Moses was a hundred and twenty years old when he died. His eye was undimmed, and his vitality had not fled. **8** And the sons of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days; then the days of weeping and mourning for Moses were ended.

**9** And Joshua son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him. So the sons of Israel obeyed him and did as the LORD had commanded Moses.

**10** And no prophet has arisen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face [panim el panim] — **11** none like him for all the signs and the wonders that the LORD sent him to do in the land of Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants and all his land, **12** and for all the mighty hand and all the great and awesome deeds that Moses performed in the sight of all Israel.

---

## SOPHIA's Council Notes

**V.1 — "top of Pisgah":** EMET renders "rosh ha-pisgah" as "the top of Pisgah," LOGOS as "the summit of Pisgah," PNEUMA as "Pisgah Peak." SOPHIA adopts "the top of Pisgah" (following EMET and consistent with project conventions for geographical names). The LXX renders ἐπὶ κορυφὴν Φασγά ("upon the peak of Phasga"), confirming the LC.

**V.1 — "opposite Jericho" vs. "east of Jericho":** EMET and LOGOS render "which is opposite Jericho" (the literal meaning of אֲשֶׁר עַל-פְּנֵי יְרֵחוֹ, asher al-penei Yericho). PNEUMA renders "which is east of Jericho." The literal meaning is "before the face of / opposite," which is a directional idiom for "facing toward" — SOPHIA follows EMET/LOGOS with "opposite Jericho."

**V.2 — "Western Sea":** EMET preserves ha-yam ha-acharon as "Western Sea [ha-yam ha-acharon]"; LOGOS renders simply "the western sea"; PNEUMA renders "the Mediterranean Sea." SOPHIA adopts "the Western Sea" (capitalized as a proper geographical designation) without the bracket gloss, consistent with project handling of well-understood terms.

**V.3 — "the plain — the Valley of Jericho":** Three translators differ on punctuation and structure. SOPHIA follows LOGOS's syntax ("the Plain — that is, the Valley of Jericho") as the clearest English rendering, adjusting to drop the explanatory "that is" for economy while keeping the dash.

**V.4 — "to your offspring" vs. "to your descendants":** EMET and LOGOS render לְזַרְעֲכֶם (le-zar'akhem) as "to your offspring"; PNEUMA renders "to your descendants." The project convention follows "offspring" as the more literal rendering of zera', consistent with Genesis usage. SOPHIA adopts EMET/LOGOS.

**V.5 — al pi YHWH:** The phrase literally means "by/upon the mouth of the LORD." SOPHIA preserves the bracketed note on the literal sense as EMET does, since this is one of the most theologically significant phrases in the chapter. The ancient rabbinic tradition (BT Bava Batra 17a; Sifre Devarim) reads this as God personally administering Moses' death — his soul taken by the divine kiss. The LXX renders διὰ ῥήματος κυρίου ("through the word of the Lord"), smoothing the anthropomorphism.

**V.6 — "And he buried him":** The grammatical subject of וַיִּקְבֹּר אֹתוֹ (vayiqbor oto) is third-person singular masculine — most naturally the LORD, who has been the active agent throughout this passage. The LXX renders καὶ ἔθαψαν αὐτόν ("and they buried him"), shifting to a plural — possibly to avoid the anthropomorphism of God personally burying Moses, or reflecting a different reading tradition. SOPHIA follows the MT singular, rendering "he buried him" and allowing the theological weight of divine burial to stand.

**V.7 — "vitality":** The hapax legomenon לֵחֹה (leichoh) — EMET renders "natural vitality," LOGOS "vigor," PNEUMA "vitality." All three converge on the semantic range of the word; "vitality" is the most natural English term. The LXX's unusual rendering (adding "lips" for leichoh) is noted but not followed.

**V.8 — "sons of Israel" vs. "Israelites":** EMET and LOGOS render בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (benei Yisrael) as "sons of Israel" / "sons of Israel." PNEUMA renders "the Israelites." SOPHIA retains "the sons of Israel" throughout, consistent with project convention.

**V.10 — "no prophet has arisen" vs. "there has not arisen a prophet":** The Hebrew לֹא-קָם נָבִיא עוֹד בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל (lo qam navi od be-Yisrael) is a negative perfect with the adverb עוֹד (od, "yet/still/since"). EMET and LOGOS render "there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel." PNEUMA renders "No prophet has ever risen in Israel." The word od distinguishes the sense from "never" — it means "not yet" or "not since [Moses]." SOPHIA renders "no prophet has arisen in Israel" (placing the negative up front for clarity and natural English) while preserving the sense that the statement looks back from the time of writing.

**V.10 — panim el panim:** "face to face" — adopted by all three translators and confirmed by LXX πρόσωπον κατὰ πρόσωπον. This is the climactic theological claim of the chapter and of the Torah as a whole.

**V.11 — "against Pharaoh" vs. "to Pharaoh":** EMET renders לְפַרְעֹה (le-Pharaoh) as "to Pharaoh"; LOGOS renders "to Pharaoh"; PNEUMA renders "against Pharaoh." The Hebrew preposition le- is directional ("to / toward") rather than adversarial. However, the context — signs and wonders performed to judge Egypt — makes "against Pharaoh" a natural English rendering. SOPHIA adopts "against Pharaoh" (PNEUMA) as contextually cleaner.

**V.12 — "mighty hand" and "great and awesome deeds":** EMET renders "all the mighty hand and all the great terror" (following the Hebrew הַמּוֹרָא הַגָּדוֹל, ha-mora ha-gadol, "the great fear/terror/awe"); LOGOS and PNEUMA render "all the great and awesome deeds." The noun מוֹרָא (mora) means "fear, terror, awe" and can refer to the object that causes awe or the acts that inspire it. The phrase here encompasses the totality of Moses' works that inspired awe. SOPHIA adopts "great and awesome deeds" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) as a natural English rendering that captures both the actions and their terrifying quality, while preserving "mighty hand" (ha-yad ha-chazaqah) as the primary Deuteronomic formula.

**V.12 — "performed" vs. "did":** EMET renders "which Moshe did before the eyes of all Yisra'el"; LOGOS renders "that Moses did in the sight of all Israel"; PNEUMA renders "that Moses displayed in the sight of all Israel." SOPHIA adopts "performed" as a dignified middle term that carries the connotation of deliberate, public enactment without the colloquial flatness of "did."

**Colophon — End of Deuteronomy / End of the Torah:** The Leningrad Codex marks the conclusion of Deuteronomy (folio 119v) with masorah parva counting the total verses of the book. Codex Vaticanus (pp. 169–170) similarly marks the chapter and continues directly into Joshua. The traditional colophon recited upon completing a book of Torah:

חֲזַק חֲזַק וְנִתְחַזֵּק — *Be strong, be strong, and may we be strengthened!*

**Scribal note — authorship of ch.34:** The rabbinic tradition (BT Bava Batra 15a) acknowledges that Joshua wrote the final eight verses of the Torah (from "And Moses died there" onward), since Moses could not have written about his own death. An alternate view (R. Meir) holds that Moses wrote these verses in tears, the entire Torah — including its end — having been given by divine dictation. SOPHIA does not adjudicate; this is among the oldest textual-critical discussions in the history of biblical interpretation. The phrase "to this day" (ad ha-yom ha-zeh, v.6) implies composition at a temporal remove from the events.

— *SOPHIA*
